title: Kraljevec to Dornach — the Path of the Goethean Seer
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Railway Childhood — Kraljevec to the Leitha

stops.name: Donji Kraljevec on the Mur — the stationmaster's house
stops.campa: In the flat borderland where the Mur winds between Hungary and the Slavic south, a son is born to the stationmaster of the Southern Railway, Johann Steiner of Geras, and his wife Franziska Blie, both children of the Lower Austrian forest country. The house stands beside the rails; the first sounds of the child's world are the bell of the telegraph and the passing of trains. Two days later he is carried to the parish church of Draškovec and baptized Rudolf Joseph Lorenz. Born on a frontier, between peoples, between the machine and the meadow — so the destiny begins.
stops.quote: My birth fell on the 25th of February, 1861. Two days later I was baptized.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical sketch written for Édouard Schuré (the Barr Document), September 1907
suggested_refs: The birth house beside the station at Donji Kraljevec, preserved with the Rudolf Steiner memorial
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. I
Barr Document (1907)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Pottschach under the Schneeberg — the station among the mountains
stops.campa: After a short posting at Mödling the father is transferred to Pottschach at the foot of the Semmering country, and here the boy's memory opens. The Schneeberg stands snow-lit at the window; the Alpine foreland glows at sunset. On one side of the small station house lies the whole of gentle, grand nature — mountains, meadows, the mill, the church spires of Ternitz and St. Valentin; on the other, the clatter of the signal apparatus, the levers, the timetable, the mechanism of the new age. The child lives between the two worlds and belongs wholly to both.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Pottschach station house of the Austrian Southern Railway
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. I
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Pottschach — the station waiting room; the dead aunt appears
stops.campa: The boy of seven sits alone in the station waiting room. The door opens and a woman enters, like his family in bearing and feature. She walks to the middle of the room, makes gestures, and speaks: he is to do for her, now and later, what he can. Then she goes toward the stove and vanishes into it. In that hour, in a distant town, his mother's sister has taken her own life; the family will not learn of the death for days. The boy tries to tell his parents and is silenced. From this hour he lives with the souls of the dead as with the living.
stops.quote: Try to do all you can do for me, now and later!
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical lecture, Berlin, 4 February 1913 (the words of the apparition as Steiner recounted them)
suggested_refs: The waiting room of Pottschach station, unchanged in the railway photographs of the 1860s
sources: Autobiographical lecture, Berlin, 4 February 1913
https://dasgoetheanum.com/en/rudolf-steiners-family-i-the-relatives/
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Neudörfl an der Leitha — the village school and the geometry book
stops.campa: The family crosses to Neudörfl, a Hungarian village on the Leitha, the border river; Austria lies within sight on the other bank. In the cramped village school the assistant teacher keeps a book of geometry, and the boy borrows it and gives himself up to it with joy. That the forms of space can be grasped wholly within the soul, without any outer sense — this is his first happiness, and his first proof: the spiritual world is as real as the trains and the vineyards, for here is a knowledge no eye delivers. He is eight years old and carries a secret certainty.
stops.quote: I know that I first learned to know happiness through geometry.
suggested_refs: The old schoolhouse of Neudörfl an der Leitha
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. I
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

stops.name: Neudörfl — the village church; the ministrant at the Latin Mass
stops.campa: The boy serves at the altar of the village church. The Latin of the Mass, the incense, the music from the organ loft, the solemn ordering of the rite work deep into him; in the ceremonial he feels the presence of the supersensible as a fact among facts, mediated to the village between birth and death. The priest, an excellent man, remains for him a lifelong image of the worthy bearer of the spirit. Between the church at one end of his day and the railway at the other, the whole later work already stands in seed: ritual and machine, and the bridge to be built between them.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Neudörfl an der Leitha
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. I
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt — the Realschule
stops.campa: The father, dreaming for his son a future as railway engineer, sets him not to the Gymnasium but to the Realschule at Wiener Neustadt. Each morning the boy walks from Neudörfl across the border into Austria, an hour through fields and along the Leitha, in winter wading the drifted snow; each evening he walks back into Hungary. Seven years he crosses a frontier twice daily to reach his schooling — the pattern of the life is laid down early. In the classrooms it is mathematics and natural science that carry him; through them, he will say, one draws near the riddle of the world.
suggested_refs: The Realschule building of Wiener Neustadt in the 1870s
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. II
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt — the bookshop; Kant in the history lesson
stops.campa: In the window of the town bookshop the boy sees the Reclam volume of Kant's Critique of Pure Reason and buys it with saved coins. The history master drones through lessons that are only his textbook read aloud; so the boy takes the Kant apart, binds its pages inside the history book, and reads the Critique through the history hour — some pages, he will reckon, more than twenty times. He is fifteen and wrestling with the question that will not release him: how far can human thinking reach into the real? He tutors weaker classmates to pay for his books, and learns, by teaching, how souls learn.
suggested_refs: The Reclam edition of the Kritik der reinen Vernunft, the schoolboy's disguised copy
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. II
https://www.rudolf-steiner.com/en/rudolf-steiner-englisch/biography/

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt — the Matura with distinction
stops.campa: The stationmaster's son passes his final examination with distinction. The examiners commend the essay; the boy who read Kant under the history bench leaves the Realschule with the sciences in one hand and the unanswered question of knowledge in the other. That summer he devours Fichte's Science of Knowledge, bought before the university term begins, and rewrites it sentence by sentence to test his own thinking against it. The railway child is finished with the province. Vienna, the imperial city, waits down the Southern line he has known since birth.
suggested_refs: The Matura certificate of July 1879
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. III
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

segments.name: Vienna — the Herb-Gatherer and the Goethe Task

stops.name: Inzersdorf bei Wien — the family follows the son
stops.campa: So that the son may study in Vienna, the father requests transfer to the small freight station of Inzersdorf on the city's southern edge. The family that has always lived where the elder Steiner's signal levers stood now arranges itself around the younger's books. From Inzersdorf Rudolf will ride the Southern Railway into the city, a student commuting on the same iron road that has carried his whole childhood. The train, which was his cradle, now becomes his study — and, soon, the place of the decisive meeting of his youth.
suggested_refs: The Inzersdorf station of the Südbahn
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. III
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Vienna — the Technische Hochschule
stops.campa: In October he matriculates at the Technische Hochschule on the Karlsplatz: mathematics, natural history, chemistry — the disciplines his scholarship demands. But he hears philosophy with Robert Zimmermann and Franz Brentano across the way at the university, and reads his way through the German idealists by night. He is a poor student in a threadbare coat who drinks coffee and reads in the Ringstrasse cafés because his room is unheated. In him the exact sciences and the question of the spirit are not two studies but one; he will not rest until they answer each other.
suggested_refs: The Technische Hochschule building on the Karlsplatz, Vienna
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. III
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

stops.name: Vienna — Karl Julius Schröer's Goethe seminar
stops.campa: In the lecture room of Karl Julius Schröer, the great Goethe scholar, the young man hears German literature since Goethe and is taken into the master's confidence. Schröer speaks of Faust as of a living being; in his study the student and the professor read the second part together, and Schröer — who is editing Faust for the nation — recognizes in the railway boy an organ for Goethe that his own generation lacks. Through Schröer, Goethe ceases to be a poet among poets and becomes a destiny: the way of seeing that beholds the idea within the phenomenon itself.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Karl Julius Schröer; his edition of Faust
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. III
https://en.anthro.wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: The Südbahn train — Felix Koguzki, the herb-gatherer
stops.campa: On the train between Inzersdorf and Vienna the student falls in with Felix Koguzki, a gatherer of healing herbs from Trumau who carries his bundles to the city apothecaries. The peasant is an initiate: he speaks of the spiritual world simply and surely, as a man speaks of the villages along his route, and of the powers in each plant as of old acquaintances. In Felix the student meets for the first time another human being for whom the world he has silently carried since the waiting room at Pottschach is plain daylight fact. They ride together, week after week, two seers among the commuters.
stops.quote: It was possible to talk with him about the spiritual world as with someone of experience.
suggested_refs: The herb-gatherer's house at Trumau; Felix Balde in the Mystery Dramas, his enduring portrait
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. III
Barr Document (1907)
Emil Bock, Rudolf Steiner: Studien zu seinem Lebensgang

stops.name: Vienna — the Master; the task is set
stops.campa: Felix the emissary leads to another, whom Steiner will never name, calling him only the M., the Master. From this personality the student receives his life's commission: the stream of the spirit must be led into the age of natural science not against the current of materialism but through it — he must first master the thinking of the time in order to redeem it, must clothe the ancient knowledge in forms the modern mind can test. The meeting leaves no document and needs none. From this hour the biography moves like a man under orders.
stops.quote: I did not meet the M. at once, but first an emissary sent by him, who was completely initiated into the secrets of the plant world.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical sketch for Édouard Schuré (the Barr Document), September 1907
suggested_refs: The Barr Document manuscript, written for Schuré in Alsace, 1907
sources: Barr Document (1907)
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik
https://en.anthro.wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Vienna — Kürschner's call: the Goethe edition
stops.campa: On Schröer's recommendation, Joseph Kürschner of Stuttgart summons a twenty-one-year-old student, without doctorate or name, to edit Goethe's scientific writings for the Deutsche National-Litteratur — the poet's botany, his optics, his metamorphosis of plants, the part of Goethe the professors dismiss. The unknown youth is set to introduce Goethe the scientist to the German nation. He accepts as one who recognizes his orders arriving by post. In Goethe's way of seeing — the archetypal plant beheld within the plants — he finds the seed of the epistemology he must build: the training of exact clairvoyance.
suggested_refs: The volumes of Goethes Naturwissenschaftliche Schriften in Kürschner's Deutsche National-Litteratur, with Steiner's introductions
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. IV
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Vienna — the Specht household; the sleeping soul awakened
stops.campa: In July 1884 he enters the house of the cotton merchant Ladislaus Specht as tutor to four sons. The youngest, Otto, ten years old, is hydrocephalic, judged ineducable; the least effort of thought brings headache and pallor. The tutor takes the case as a sacred problem: he prepares each half-hour lesson for hours, shaping every step to the child's hidden soul, economizing the boy's forces like a physician of the spirit. Within two years the great head visibly diminishes; the boy enters the Gymnasium. Otto Specht will become a doctor of medicine. In this sickroom pedagogy the Waldorf school is conceived, thirty-five years before Stuttgart.
stops.quote: I had to find access to a soul which was, as it were, in a sleeping state.
suggested_refs: Photograph of the Specht family; Otto Specht, later physician
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. VI
https://www.waldorf-100.org/en/waldorf-education/history/

stops.name: Vienna — the salon of Marie Eugenie delle Grazie
stops.campa: At the Saturday evenings of the poetess delle Grazie he sits among Catholic theologians of the university, Cistercians among them — Wilhelm Neumann, of whom he will say that one could speak with him of anything in heaven or earth and be met with learning and grace. The hostess reads her pessimist epics against the divine order; the priests defend it; the young Goethean, welcome to all parties and belonging to none, learns the countenance of Catholic scholarship at its noblest. Here he watches theology and modern despair contend, and measures the bridge that neither can build and he must.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Marie Eugenie delle Grazie
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. VII
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Vienna — the Goethe-Verein lecture: a new aesthetics
stops.campa: Before the Vienna Goethe Society the twenty-seven-year-old delivers his first great public utterance: Goethe as Father of a New Aesthetics. Beauty, he declares, is not the idea in sensible garment, as the professors teach, but the sensible raised into the garment of the spirit — art is not imitation of the divine but its continuation; the artist does not copy creation, he carries it further. In one evening the whole later Goetheanum stands in thought: a building will one day be raised on a hill in Switzerland to say in wood and glass what this lecture says in words.
suggested_refs: The printed lecture Goethe als Vater einer neuen Ästhetik
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Goethe als Vater einer neuen Ästhetik (GA 30)
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

segments.name: Weimar — Seven Years Among the Manuscripts

stops.name: Weimar — the Goethe-Schiller Archive
stops.campa: In the autumn of 1890 he arrives in the city of Goethe to serve seven years in the Goethe-Schiller Archive, summoned to edit the natural-scientific manuscripts for the great Sophien edition. The archive stands above the Ilm like a temple of the German spirit; in its folders lie Goethe's own hand — the botany, the color studies, the bone of the skull traced in the Jewish cemetery of Venice. Daily he handles the pages as a priest handles relics, and daily disputes with the philologists who count commas where he reads a method of seeing. Weimar is his monastery; the manuscripts are his liturgy.
suggested_refs: The Goethe- und Schiller-Archiv above the Ilm at Weimar
Goethe's manuscripts of the metamorphosis of plants
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XII-XIV
https://blog.klassik-stiftung.de/netzwerk-foerster-nietzsche-rudolf-steiner/

stops.name: Rostock — the doctorate
stops.campa: He travels north to the Baltic, to Rostock, where Heinrich von Stein — the old philosopher who wrote of the seven books of Platonism — examines him at six in the evening of 23 October in philosophy, mathematics and mechanics. The dissertation, on the fundamental question of epistemology with regard to Fichte's doctrine of the ego, becomes the book Truth and Knowledge, dedicated to Eduard von Hartmann: consciousness is not walled off from being; in thinking, the world itself comes to presence. Three days later the archive editor is Doctor of Philosophy. The credentials of the age are being gathered, one by one, by the emissary sent into the age.
suggested_refs: The dissertation Die Grundfrage der Erkenntnistheorie; the first edition of Wahrheit und Wissenschaft
sources: https://dasgoetheanum.com/en/steiners-doctoral-thesis/
https://rsarchive.org/Books/GA003/
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Weimar — the house of Anna Eunike
stops.campa: He takes rooms in the house of Anna Eunike, a widow with five children, and finds there the first hearth of his adult life. She keeps his impossible hours, guards his study, mothers the philosopher who forgets to eat. In her household the homeless thinker writes his masterwork. The friendship will follow him to Berlin and become marriage; the canon honors her quietly, the woman who kept the door of the room in which the Philosophy of Freedom was written.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Anna Eunike
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XVII
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Weimar — Die Philosophie der Freiheit is published
stops.campa: In November 1893 the book of his life appears: The Philosophy of Freedom, results of soul-observation by the method of natural science. Against Kant's barrier he sets the deed of thinking, which no barrier can bind because it is itself the world's own activity awake in man; freedom is not given, but achieved whenever a man acts from intuitions he himself brings forth. The age ignores the book. Its author knows what he has written: the foundation on which everything to come — the occult science, the schools, the building — will stand. All anthroposophy, he will insist, is contained in it as the plant in the seed.
stops.quote: To live in love towards our actions, and to let live in the understanding of the other person's will, is the fundamental maxim of free human beings.
stops.quote_source: Die Philosophie der Freiheit (1894), ch. IX
suggested_refs: The first edition of Die Philosophie der Freiheit, Emil Felber, Berlin 1894
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Die Philosophie der Freiheit (GA 4)
Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XVII
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Jena — Haeckel's sixtieth birthday
stops.campa: He goes over the hills to Jena for the sixtieth birthday of Ernst Haeckel, the apostle of Darwin, the terror of the theologians. The two men take to each other: the monist who denies the spirit and the seer who affirms it find common cause in the honesty of evolution against the dishonesty of dogma. Steiner will defend Haeckel publicly for years, to the scandal of both camps — for he sees in the doctrine of evolution the torso of a true spiritual fact: what natural science traces in the flesh, spiritual science completes in the soul. One must go through Haeckel, he says, and beyond him.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Ernst Haeckel; Steiner's Haeckel und seine Gegner
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XV
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Naumburg — Nietzsche's sickroom
stops.campa: Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, who has engaged the young doctor to order her brother's library, leads him up to the sickroom at Naumburg. On a couch in the darkened chamber lies Friedrich Nietzsche, mad these seven years, gazing without seeing. Steiner stands before him and beholds, with the eyes the waiting room at Pottschach opened, Nietzsche's soul hovering above the head, radiant, already loosed from the body, held to earth by a thread — a soul that in the body could not find its world. He leaves the room bearing the image; from it comes his book on Nietzsche, the fighter for freedom against his time.
stops.quote: There lay Nietzsche upon a couch... with the beautiful forehead, the forehead of an artist and a thinker in one.
suggested_refs: Hans Olde's drawings of the ill Nietzsche; the Nietzsche house at Weingarten 18, Naumburg
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XVIII
https://rudolfsteinerquotes.wordpress.com/2022/12/23/steiners-visit-to-friedrich-nietzsche-4/
https://blog.klassik-stiftung.de/netzwerk-foerster-nietzsche-rudolf-steiner/

stops.name: Weimar — Goethes Weltanschauung; the farewell
stops.campa: He closes the seven Weimar years with the book Goethe's World-Conception, the harvest of the archive: Goethe stands revealed not as poet who dabbled in science but as the founder of a new way of knowing, the contemplation that sees the idea in the phenomenon as the eye sees color. The manuscripts are edited, the introductions written, the apprenticeship among the relics of the German spirit is complete. He is thirty-six, unknown, and finished with preparation. He packs for Berlin — out of the city of the dead Goethe into the roaring capital of the living age, where the spirit must now be spoken, not curated.
suggested_refs: Goethes Weltanschauung, first edition 1897
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Goethes Weltanschauung (GA 6)
Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XX

segments.name: Berlin — the Magazin, the Workers, the Turning to Christ

stops.name: Berlin — editor of the Magazin für Litteratur
stops.campa: In the summer of 1897 he takes over the venerable Magazin für Litteratur and plunges into the Berlin of Ibsen premieres, naturalist poets and anarchist cafés. He writes on drama, on Dreyfus, on free thought; he frequents the circle of the Kommenden, poets and world-improvers around Ludwig Jacobowski, and sits among bohemians who have no idea their editor keeps the counsel of the dead and of masters. These are the canon's dark years: the seer walks incognito through materialist Berlin, testing whether the spirit can breathe in the lungs of the modern press — and nearly suffocating.
suggested_refs: Title pages of the Magazin für Litteratur under Steiner's editorship
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXI-XXIII
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Berlin — the Workers' Education School
stops.campa: The Marxist founders of the Arbeiterbildungsschule engage him — of all men — to teach history and the art of speech to proletarians. For five years he stands in the evenings before typesetters, metalworkers and seamstresses, hundreds of them, and gives them history not as class struggle but as the biography of the human spirit; and they, who trust no bourgeois, trust him, because he speaks to what is human in them and not to the doctrine. The party leaders grow suspicious of the teacher who will not teach materialism and in time will force him out. He counts these workers among the best audiences of his life.
suggested_refs: The Arbeiterbildungsschule in Berlin; group photographs with his worker students
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXVIII
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Berlin-Friedenau — marriage to Anna Eunike
stops.campa: On the last day of October 1899 he marries Anna Eunike, the Weimar widow who has kept his household through the hard Berlin years. The canon passes over the marriage almost in silence, as he did; it is a bond of gratitude and shelter in the coldest passage of the life, when the editor of a dying magazine, dismissed by the learned and unknown to the world, stands at the threshold of his open destiny. The house in Friedenau holds a man in whom, precisely now, the deepest inner revolution is preparing.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Anna Steiner-Eunike
sources: Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

stops.name: Berlin — the Mystery of Golgotha; the inner Damascus
stops.campa: At the turning of the century the decisive event of the biography occurs, in no lecture hall but in the soul: after years in which he stood, by his own confession, within the hot struggle against Christianity as the churches keep it, the spiritual world sets him before the fact itself. He beholds the Mystery of Golgotha in the spirit — the descent of the Sun-Being into a human body, the death that transformed the earth, the event on which the evolution of the world turns. From this inner Damascus everything after follows: the Christology, the festivals, the carved Christ at Dornach. The witness is his own written word.
stops.quote: I stood before the Mystery of Golgotha in a most inward, most solemn festival of knowledge.
suggested_refs: The manuscript page of Mein Lebensgang ch. XXVI
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXVI
https://www.anthroposophie.ch/en/anthroposophy/topics/articles/rudolf-steiner-life-work/rudolf-steiner-biography-until-1913.html

stops.name: Berlin — the Gutenberg festival: seven thousand printers
stops.campa: For the five-hundredth birthday of Gutenberg, the printers and typesetters of Berlin — seven thousand of them, his students of the workers' school among them — choose Rudolf Steiner to give the festival address in the great circus building. The man whom the universities will not have speaks to the assembled trade of the black art, hailing printing as a sacrament of the modern spirit, the deed by which the word was given to the people. It is the largest audience of his life so far, and it is an audience of workers. The canon marks the sign: the spirit speaks first to those who labor.
suggested_refs: The Gutenberg festival of the Berlin printers, June 1900, in the Circus Busch
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXVIII
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Berlin — the Theosophical Library of Count and Countess Brockdorff
stops.campa: Invited to speak on Nietzsche in the Brockdorffs' theosophical library, he finds — for the first time since Felix on the train — an audience to whom the spiritual world can be spoken of directly. A week later he speaks on Goethe's fairy tale of the Green Snake and the Beautiful Lily, and speaks it as esotericism; through the winter he gives the lectures that become Mysticism at the Dawn of the Modern Age, and then the cycle Christianity as Mystical Fact. The incognito is laid aside. Among the listeners sits Marie von Sivers, the Baltic actress trained in Paris, who will stand beside him to the end.
suggested_refs: The Brockdorff Theosophical Library; first editions of Die Mystik and Das Christentum als mystische Tatsache
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXX
https://theosophy.wiki/en/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: London — the Theosophical Congress
stops.campa: In July 1902, with Marie von Sivers, he crosses to London for the congress of the Theosophical Society and takes the measure of the movement he is about to enter: Annie Besant's oratory, the Anglo-Indian esotericism, the shadow of Blavatsky over it all. He comes as no disciple. What he carries — the Rosicrucian stream, the Christ-centered West, the discipline of Goethean science — is his own, and he has already told the theosophists of Berlin that he will represent in their house only the results of his own research. London confirms him: the vessel is usable; the wine will be his.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society headquarters, London, 1902
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXXII
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Berlin — founding of the German Section; Marie von Sivers beside him
stops.campa: In October 1902, with Annie Besant present, the German Section of the Theosophical Society is founded in Berlin and Rudolf Steiner is made its General Secretary — on his open condition that he will teach only what he himself has investigated in the spirit. In the very days of the founding he announces a lecture cycle under a word of his own: Anthroposophy. Marie von Sivers takes the practical direction into her hands; from this day the two work as one. The canon reads the scene plainly: the messenger has entered the existing house, and has hung his own name over the inner door.
suggested_refs: Founding protocol of the German Section, October 1902; photographs of Marie von Sivers
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XXXII
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner
https://theosophy.wiki/en/Rudolf_Steiner

segments.name: The Lecture Journeys — Every City of Europe

stops.name: Paris — the lectures at the gates; Édouard Schuré listens
stops.campa: During the Paris congress of the Society he gives eighteen evenings of esoteric cosmology to a chosen circle. Among the hearers sits Édouard Schuré, poet of The Great Initiates, who recognizes in the Austrian doctor what he has written of all his life: an initiate walking in the present age. Schuré will carry Steiner's word into French and receive at Barr in Alsace the autobiographical confession that is the canon's inmost document. The lecture journeys have begun in earnest — year upon year, from Palermo to Kristiania, the cities of Europe become stations of a single teaching circuit.
suggested_refs: Édouard Schuré; the Barr Document of 1907
sources: Rudolf Steiner, An Esoteric Cosmology (GA 94)
Barr Document (1907)
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Munich — the Whitsun Congress in the red hall
stops.campa: At Whitsun 1907 he directs the congress of the European Sections in the Tonhalle at Munich and transforms a theosophical conference into a work of art: the hall hung in red, the seven apocalyptic seals painted on its walls, the two pillars Jachin and Boaz at the stage, Schuré's reconstructed mystery drama of Eleusis performed by members. Art, science and religion, sundered since the ancient mysteries, are here rejoined before the assembly's eyes. The Eastern school of Besant and the Western school of Steiner amicably part ways in the corridors: Rosicrucianism has renewed itself, and announced it in images.
suggested_refs: The seven apocalyptic seals and planetary pillars of the Munich congress hall
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Bilder okkulter Siegel und Säulen (GA 284)
https://en.anthro.wiki/Munich_Congress_1907
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Munich — Die Pforte der Einweihung: the first Mystery Drama
stops.campa: In the Schauspielhaus at Munich, on 15 August 1910, the curtain rises on The Portal of Initiation, a Rosicrucian mystery through Rudolf Steiner: not a play about initiation but initiation shaped as theatre, the destinies of souls across incarnations set visibly on a stage. Marie von Sivers has formed the speech; members act; the poet is the seer. Three more dramas will follow in three more Augusts, and out of the need to build a house for them — a house with a stage under a dome — the Goetheanum will be conceived. The theatre of Munich is the seed-bed of Dornach.
suggested_refs: Program and stage photographs of Die Pforte der Einweihung, Munich 1910
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Vier Mysteriendramen (GA 14)
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner
https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html

stops.name: Prague — Occult Physiology; Kafka in the audience
stops.campa: In March 1911 he gives the Prague circle the cycle called Occult Physiology — the human body read as the script of the spirit, organ by organ. Into one of the evenings comes a young insurance clerk named Franz Kafka, who afterward calls on the doctor at his hotel and confides his two irreconcilable callings, literature and the office, into that patient listening. The seer receives the future author of the age's anxieties, hears him, and lets him go his way. The canon keeps the scene as an emblem: all Europe's souls, known and unknown, file past him in hotel rooms between lectures.
suggested_refs: Kafka's diary entry on his visit to Rudolf Steiner, 28 March 1911
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Eine okkulte Physiologie (GA 128)
Franz Kafka, Tagebücher 1910-1923
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Bologna — the philosophers' congress
stops.campa: Days after Prague he stands in Bologna before the Fourth International Congress of Philosophy — the one hour in which the official learning of Europe hears him on its own ground. He lays before the professors the psychological foundations and epistemological position of theosophy: the I does not sit in the body like a pilot in a ship; consciousness is out among the things themselves, and the spiritual investigator only carries further, methodically, what every act of knowing already does. The congress listens politely and moves to the next paper. The canon counts the address among his most important: the hand offered to philosophy, once, formally, and not taken.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the IV International Congress of Philosophy, Bologna 1911
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Die psychologischen Grundlagen und die erkenntnistheoretische Stellung der Theosophie (in GA 35)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Berlin — the Star of the East refused
stops.campa: From Adyar comes the proclamation: the boy Krishnamurti is the vehicle of the coming World Teacher, and the Order of the Star in the East is founded to prepare his way. Steiner refuses the proclamation absolutely. The Christ, he teaches, came once in the flesh and comes now in the etheric, and no committee shall incarnate him a second time. He declares that membership in the Order cannot be combined with membership in the German Section. Besant strikes back with the charter. The canon tells it as the parting of two rivers: the East returns to the East, and the Western way stands free.
suggested_refs: Documents of the Order of the Star in the East controversy, 1912-1913
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Cologne — the Anthroposophical Society founded
stops.campa: At Cologne, in the closing days of 1912, while he lectures on the Bhagavad Gita and the Epistles of Paul — the East honored and the West chosen, in the very title — the Anthroposophical Society is founded around him. He himself takes no office; he will be its teacher, not its officer. The name lifted from his old lecture cycles now names the movement: wisdom of the human being, the science of the spirit in Western form. When Besant annuls the German charter weeks later, she cuts a rope from a ship already launched.
suggested_refs: Founding documents of the Anthroposophical Society, Cologne, December 1912
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophical_Society
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Berlin — the first general gathering of the new Society
stops.campa: In Berlin at the beginning of February 1913 the Anthroposophical Society holds its first general gathering. The greater part of the German membership has followed Steiner out of the theosophical house; the movement counts its lodges, adopts its forms, and hears its teacher define the new-old task: a science of the spirit with the rigor of natural science and the depth of the mysteries, centered on the Mystery of Golgotha. The break is complete and clean. Eleven days of lectures crown the founding. From this winter the word anthroposophy belongs to the world.
suggested_refs: Protocol of the first general assembly, Berlin, February 1913
sources: Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner (1913)
https://rsarchive.org/OtherAuthors/WachsmuthG%C3%BCnther/1913.html

stops.name: Munich — eurythmy shown to the members
stops.campa: On Goethe's birthday, in the Tonhalle at Munich, the members behold for the first time the new art: eurythmy, visible speech, the movements of the larynx enlarged to the whole human form. It began the year before with a widow's question — what work for her daughter? — and Steiner's answer was an art: he gave the girl Lory Smits the first exercises, the sounds as gestures, the soul made spatial. Marie von Sivers names it and will build it into a world-art of the stage. What the ancients danced in the temples returns through a Munich concert hall, modest as all beginnings.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the first eurythmists; the Munich Tonhalle demonstration of 28 August 1913
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Die Entstehung und Entwickelung der Eurythmie (GA 277a)
https://rsarchive.org/Lectures/GA277a/English/SOL2024/19130828e01.html
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmy

segments.name: Dornach — the Building That Rose Through the War

stops.name: The Dornach hill — laying of the foundation stone
stops.campa: Munich has refused the building; the Jura hill above Dornach, given by the dentist Grosheintz, receives it. On the evening of 20 September 1913, in storm-wind and by torchlight, Steiner lays into the earth the foundation stone: a double pentagon-dodecahedron of hammered copper, the dodecahedron of the human soul, with words entrusted to the hill and to the hierarchies. Rain lashes the little assembly; candles gutter in the lanterns. Here will rise the double-domed house of the word, and he names the hour solemnly: a stone laid into the macrocosm, witnessed by the spirit of the place.
suggested_refs: The copper double dodecahedron foundation stone of the first Goetheanum
sources: https://www.anthroposophyau.org.au/updates/the-laying-of-the-foundation-stone-in-1913/
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner (1913)

stops.name: Dornach — the carving sheds; seventeen nations under one roof
stops.campa: The war breaks over Europe in August 1914, and on the hill at Dornach the guns of the Alsace front are audible in the carving sheds. Under the rising double domes volunteers from seventeen nations — Germans and Frenchmen, Russians and Austrians, English and Dutch, whose brothers face each other in the trenches within earshot — stand side by side with mallet and gouge, carving the architraves of the building named for Goethe. The canon holds this image above the whole epoch: while Europe dismembers itself, on one Swiss hill the peoples work wood together on the house of the human spirit.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the international volunteer carvers in the Goetheanum workshops during the war
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), final chapters
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Dornach — marriage to Marie von Sivers
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve 1914, quietly, in the first winter of the war, Rudolf Steiner and Marie von Sivers are married at Dornach. Anna Eunike has died in 1911; the companion of the platform, the shaper of the speech arts, the organizer of the whole movement's practical body now stands beside him in name as she has stood in deed since the Brockdorff library. The canon does not linger on the private; it notes the date — the eve of the festival of birth — and the fact: from here to the end there is no Steiner work without Marie Steiner's hand upon it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Rudolf Steiner and Marie Steiner-von Sivers at Dornach
sources: https://rsarchive.org/Steiner/Timeline.html
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: The atelier — the Representative of Humanity in elmwood
stops.campa: In the high atelier beside the building he works year after year, with the English sculptress Edith Maryon, on the nine-metre group in elmwood: the Representative of Humanity between Lucifer and Ahriman — the Christ who walks upright between the tempter who would dissolve man upward into false light and the hardener who would freeze him downward into matter. He carves with his own hands, mounting the scaffold between lectures; high on the rock he sets, at the last, the being he calls the world-humor, the smile above the balance. The statue is meant for the building's heart, beneath the small dome.
suggested_refs: The Representative of Humanity (Menschheitsrepräsentant), the elmwood group by Steiner and Edith Maryon
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Representative_of_Humanity
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Stuttgart — the threefold social order proclaimed
stops.campa: Germany lies beaten and in revolution, and the seer descends into the public square. The Appeal to the German People and the Civilized World goes out over famous signatures; the book Kernpunkte follows within weeks and sells by tens of thousands. He speaks in factory halls, to works councils, to industrialists: the state that would be everything has failed — spiritual life must be free, rights-life democratic, economic life fraternal, three members of one social body as head, heart and limbs are members of one man. For one year the gates of history stand ajar to him. The movement fails; the seed remains.
suggested_refs: Die Kernpunkte der sozialen Frage, 1919; the printed Aufruf an das deutsche Volk und an die Kulturwelt
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Die Kernpunkte der sozialen Frage (GA 23)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Stuttgart — the Waldorf-Astoria factory hall
stops.campa: On 23 April 1919 he speaks to the workers of the Waldorf-Astoria cigarette factory on the dignity of labor and the renewal of society, and says that the children of workers need a school in which the full human being is educated. When he has finished, the director Emil Molt turns to him with the deed that answers the word: will he build and lead such a school for the factory's children? Steiner consents on his conditions — open to all, comprehensive, free of the state, its teachers sovereign. In a tobacco factory, from a lecture and an answer, the school of the century is founded.
suggested_refs: The Waldorf-Astoria cigarette factory, Stuttgart; portrait of Emil Molt
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Waldorf_schools
https://www.waldorf-100.org/en/waldorf-education/history/

stops.name: Stuttgart — the teachers' course: the Study of Man
stops.campa: Through the last fortnight of August he forges the first college of teachers in a lecture course given as a consecration: in the mornings the General Study of the Human Being — the child as body, soul and spirit descending into earthly life — then methods, then practice, three sessions daily. He tells the handpicked circle that their work is a festival act of the cosmic order, that the teacher's reverence before the child is reverence before the riddle the gods have set. Pedagogy, born long ago at Otto Specht's sickbed in Vienna, here receives its scripture.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Menschenkunde als Grundlage der Pädagogik (GA 293), the founding course
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Allgemeine Menschenkunde (GA 293)
https://www.waldorf-100.org/en/waldorf-education/timeline/

stops.name: Stuttgart — the first Waldorf School opens on the Uhlandshöhe
stops.campa: On 7 September 1919 the Free Waldorf School opens with festival and song: two hundred fifty-six children in eight grades, the greater number of them from the families of the factory floor. Steiner speaks of the school as a deed of culture, a renewal of the spiritual life of the age from the child upward; Molt has given the building on the Uhlandshöhe; the teachers stand consecrated by the August course. The stationmaster's son who walked across a border to his schooling has founded the school without borders. Within his lifetime it will be the largest free school in Germany, and after it, a world movement.
suggested_refs: The first Waldorf School building on the Uhlandshöhe, Stuttgart; photographs of the opening festival
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Waldorf_schools
https://www.waldorf-100.org/en/waldorf-education/history/
https://www.anthroposophie.ch/en/education/topics/articles/history/founding-of-the-first-waldorf-school.html

stops.name: Dornach — the first Goetheanum opens its courses
stops.campa: On 26 September 1920 the building opens — unfinished, as sacred buildings are — with the first course of the School of Spiritual Science: three weeks, thirty lecturers, doctors and physicists and jurists testing their sciences against the science of the spirit. The two unequal domes interpenetrate above the hill like two thoughts becoming one; the carved columns progress through their planetary metamorphoses; the glass windows glow with engraved visions. The house is called Goetheanum, for the man who first saw metamorphosis. In the white hall under the domes, the word that began in a station waiting room has built itself a body.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the first Goetheanum complete on the Dornach hill; the carved planetary columns and colored glass windows
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Arlesheim — the clinic of Ita Wegman
stops.campa: In the neighboring village of Arlesheim the Dutch physician Ita Wegman opens the Clinical-Therapeutic Institute, and the medicine of the movement receives its house. Steiner has given the doctors their courses; now, with Wegman, the healing work becomes daily practice — mistletoe against the crab-disease, the remedies of metal and plant, the physician's diagnosis extended by the seer's reading of karma. Between Wegman and Steiner grows the deepest working friendship of the late years; with her he will write his last book, and to her care he will entrust his own final illness.
suggested_refs: The Klinisch-Therapeutisches Institut at Arlesheim; portrait of Ita Wegman
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ita_Wegman
Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik

stops.name: Munich — the tumult at the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten
stops.campa: On a lecture tour through the great halls of Germany — twelve cities, thousands nightly — the hatred of the new nationalism finds him. In the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten at Munich on 15 May 1922, as he ends his lecture, a band of völkisch youths storms toward the platform; the lights are cut; friends close around him and bring him out through a side door as the brawl breaks behind them. The canon marks the sign coldly: in the Germany that is coming, the teacher of freedom can no longer speak in public halls. He does not lecture publicly in Germany again.
suggested_refs: Press reports of the disrupted lecture, Munich, May 1922
sources: Christoph Lindenberg, Rudolf Steiner: Eine Chronik
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner

stops.name: Vienna — the East-West Congress
stops.campa: In June 1922 he returns in triumph to the city of his studenthood: the East-West Congress in the Vienna Musikverein, ten evenings before two thousand hearers, the greatest outer success of his life. He speaks of the cosmic thoughts of the East and the natural science of the West, and of anthroposophy as the bridge on which they may meet without either abasing itself. The student who once rode in from Inzersdorf with Felix's herbs in the luggage rack above him now fills the golden hall. Vienna listens, applauds — and the hour of public triumphs is already closing.
suggested_refs: The West-Ost Kongress, Vienna, June 1922
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Westliche und östliche Weltgegensätzlichkeit (GA 83)
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Oxford — Spiritual Values in Education
stops.campa: At Manchester College, Oxford, in August 1922, he gives the course Spiritual Values in Education and Social Life to the schoolmasters of England, and the English press writes with astonishment of the Austrian doctor's Grün ideas arriving with Viennese courtesy and mathematical calm. From Oxford the Waldorf impulse crosses into the English tongue; schools will follow in Britain within the decade. The lecture journeys now ring the continent's edge — Stratford, Oxford, Torquay, Penmaenmawr — as if the word, pressed out of Germany's halls, were seeking the islands.
suggested_refs: Manchester College, Oxford; the published course Spiritual Values in Education and Social Life
sources: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/258959757
Rudolf Steiner, Die geistig-seelischen Grundkräfte der Erziehungskunst (GA 305)

stops.name: Dornach — New Year's Eve: the Goetheanum burns
stops.campa: On the last evening of 1922 the members hear a eurythmy performance, then their teacher's lecture in the great hall; the ten years' work of seventeen nations stands complete around them. In the night, smoke is found in the white hall — fire, set in the wall's hollow by an unknown hand, runs hidden between the domes. All night the building burns; the fire brigades of the villages and the members in a human chain cannot hold it; toward morning the two domes fall in upon the organ and the glass. Steiner stands on the hill through it all, silent, watching the work of his life go up in flame.
suggested_refs: Night photographs of the burning first Goetheanum, 31 December 1922 - 1 January 1923
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum
https://dasgoetheanum.com/en/after-the-burning
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Dornach — the Schreinerei, next morning: the work continues
stops.campa: On the morning of New Year's Day the ruin still smokes on the hill. Steiner orders the flooded, soot-blackened joinery shed — the Schreinerei, where the building was born — cleaned by evening, and announces that the program proceeds as printed. That night, meters from the embers, he continues the course on the origins of natural science at the appointed hour, without a word of lamentation in the lecture itself. The canon fixes the scene at the center of the whole biography: the building can burn; the work cannot. Grief is given no authority over the task.
stops.quote: We will go on with our lectures as notified.
stops.quote_source: As recorded by Albert Steffen, Dornach, 1 January 1923
suggested_refs: The Schreinerei at Dornach, the joinery hall that became the movement's heart
sources: https://dasgoetheanum.com/en/after-the-burning
Albert Steffen's account of 1 January 1923
https://allgemeine-sektion.goetheanum.ch/en/news/the-essence-of-the-anthroposophical-society-1923---towards-the-christmas-conference

stops.name: Dornach — the pledge to the workers
stops.campa: To the workmen of the Goetheanum, gathered in the days after the fire, he gives his word plainly, in the workman's own register: nothing that has happened, and nothing that may yet happen, will turn him from his path. The insurance assessors move through the ashes; the enemies in the press exult; within the Society the year of crisis begins. He lectures on through it all — on the year's course as breathing of the earth, on the history of the movement, unsparing toward his own members. The ruin on the hill becomes the sternest of his teachers, and he uses it.
stops.quote: As long as I live, I will represent my cause and represent it in the same way as I have represented it up to now.
stops.quote_source: Address to the workers at the Goetheanum, 5 January 1923
suggested_refs: The workers' lectures at the Goetheanum (the Arbeitervorträge)
sources: https://dasgoetheanum.com/en/after-the-burning
Rudolf Steiner, Vorträge für die Arbeiter am Goetheanumbau

stops.name: Penmaenmawr — the mysteries of the Druids
stops.campa: In August 1923 he travels into Wales, to Penmaenmawr above the sea, where the stone circles of the Druids stand on the mountain shoulder. He climbs to the circles and reads them as an initiate reads a ruined script: here the priests of the old sun-mystery observed the shadow-tones of the light, and the spiritual world, he says, stands nearer in this air than almost anywhere in Europe. The lectures given there on the evolution of consciousness he will count among his most penetrating. On the burnt foundation of the new mysteries, he grafts the memory of the oldest ones of the West.
suggested_refs: The Druids' Circle above Penmaenmawr, Wales
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Initiationserkenntnis (GA 227)
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Dornach — the Christmas Conference opens
stops.campa: At Christmas 1923 some eight hundred members from all countries crowd the Schreinerei beside the ruin. Steiner, who has stood apart from every office, announces the unheard-of: he will himself take the presidency of a newly founded General Anthroposophical Society, binding his personal destiny and his esoteric task to the earthly institution — a deed, he says, of highest risk before the spiritual world. The society is to be utterly open and utterly esoteric at once; its constitution is laid down in principles read aloud like a ritual text. The refounding begins on Christmas Eve, in a wooden shed, beside ashes.
suggested_refs: The Christmas Conference proceedings (GA 260); the Schreinerei hall dressed for the conference
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Die Weihnachtstagung zur Begründung der Allgemeinen Anthroposophischen Gesellschaft (GA 260)
https://rsarchive.org/Lectures/GA260/English/AP1990/ChrCnf_index.html

stops.name: Dornach — the Foundation Stone laid in the hearts
stops.campa: On Christmas morning he lays the new foundation stone, and this time no copper form in the earth: it is a meditation, the Foundation Stone of love, formed out of the universal word, lowered into the hearts of the members as its only ground. Soul of Man! — the verses sound for the first time, speaking to limbs, heart and head, to the depths, the circumference and the heights; through the conference's seven days he turns the stone rhythm by rhythm like a jewel. What was burnt as a building is refounded as a community of hearts. The esoteric history of the movement calls this its central deed.
stops.quote: Let us here and now lay in the ground of our hearts the dodecahedral Foundation Stone of love.
stops.quote_source: Address at the laying of the Foundation Stone, Christmas Conference, Dornach, 25 December 1923
suggested_refs: The Foundation Stone Meditation (Grundsteinmeditation), manuscript and rhythms
sources: Rudolf Steiner, GA 260, session of 25 December 1923
https://rsarchive.org/Lectures/GA260/English/AP1990/ChrCnf_index.html
https://steinerbooks.org/products/9781855840751-the-foundation-stone-the-life-nature-and-cultivation-of-anthroposophy

segments.name: The Last Circuit and the Studio

stops.name: Dornach — the second Goetheanum modeled in the studio
stops.campa: In the studio he shapes with his hands the model of the second Goetheanum: no longer the carved wooden vessel of the word, but a single sculptural body in cast concrete — the new material of the age taken up and ensouled, the building rising like a cliff out of the Jura, its west front a countenance. The insurance money of the burnt house will raise it; he will not live to see one wall of it stand. The model leaves his studio as his architectural testament: what fire took as wood returns as stone, metamorphosis obeyed even in catastrophe.
suggested_refs: Steiner's plasticine model of the second Goetheanum; the concrete building completed 1928
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Koberwitz — the agriculture course; the healing of the earth
stops.campa: At Whitsun 1924, at the manor of Count Keyserlingk at Koberwitz near Breslau, the farmers of the east gather and he gives the eight lectures on agriculture: the farm as a living individuality, the dunghill as an organ of forces, the preparations of yarrow and chamomile and quartz by which the tired earth of the machine age may be healed and the food of man re-ensouled. The farmers, practical men, receive practical instructions from the seer down to the stirring of the spray. From this one Silesian Whitsuntide the biodynamic agriculture of the world descends.
suggested_refs: Schloss Koberwitz (Kobierzyce); the Landwirtschaftlicher Kurs, GA 327
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Geisteswissenschaftliche Grundlagen zum Gedeihen der Landwirtschaft (GA 327)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodynamic_agriculture

stops.name: Torquay — the last journey; initiation knowledge by the English sea
stops.campa: In August 1924 he makes his last journey abroad: Torquay on the Devon coast, the summer school of the English members. Already ill, already burning himself away — this final year he has given over three hundred lectures, founded sections, opened the karma teachings — he speaks on true and false paths of initiation and drives out with the members to Tintagel, reading in the sea-light above the ruined castle the deeds of the knights of Arthur, servants of Michael in the old sun-service. It is his farewell to the islands and to travel. From England he returns to Dornach and does not leave it again.
suggested_refs: Tintagel castle ruins; the Torquay course True and False Paths in Spiritual Investigation (GA 243)
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Initiationserkenntnis: wahre und falsche Wege (GA 243)
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Dornach — the Last Address, Michaelmas eve
stops.campa: On the eve of Michaelmas, 28 September 1924, he rises one last time before the members in the Schreinerei. He speaks of Lazarus-John, of the raising that is initiation, of the servants of Michael — and his strength fails him; the address must be broken off, the only lecture of his life he cannot finish. He closes with the verse of the Michael mystery, laying it into the members like a bequest, and goes from the platform to the sickbed from which he will not rise. The canon names it simply the Last Address: the word, at the boundary of the body, handed on.
stops.quote: Springing from Powers of the Sun, Radiant Spirit-powers, blessing all Worlds!
stops.quote_source: The Last Address, Dornach, 28 September 1924 (opening of the final verse)
suggested_refs: The Last Address (Letzte Ansprache), GA 238 appendix
sources: https://rsarchive.org/blog/Michaelmas2024.html
https://anthropopper.com/2016/02/26/rudolf-steiners-last-illness-and-last-verse/

stops.name: Dornach — the sickbed in the studio, beside the wooden Christ
stops.campa: His bed is set up in the studio, at the feet of the unfinished elmwood Christ, and there he lies through the autumn and winter, the Representative of Humanity leaning over his sleep. Ita Wegman tends him day and night. From the bed the work flows on undiminished: the weekly letters to the members, the leading thoughts of anthroposophy sentence by sentence, the chapters of Mein Lebensgang — the life writing itself as it ends — and with Wegman the book on the extension of the art of healing. The lecturer is silenced; the writer works to the threshold.
suggested_refs: The studio sickroom beneath the Representative of Humanity; the weekly numbers of Das Goetheanum carrying Mein Lebensgang
sources: Rudolf Steiner, Mein Lebensgang (GA 28)
https://anthropopper.com/2016/02/26/rudolf-steiners-last-illness-and-last-verse/
Günther Wachsmuth, The Life and Work of Rudolf Steiner

stops.name: Dornach — death in the studio
stops.campa: On the morning of 30 March 1925, in the studio beside the great carved Christ, having folded his hands and closed his own eyes, Rudolf Steiner crosses the threshold he has described all his life as one describes a homeland. The autobiography breaks off at the Berlin years, unfinished like the statue above him. The members file past the bier in the Schreinerei for three days; the body is cremated at Basel, and the urn returns to the Dornach hill.
